title: How do we find the area of an isosceles triangle from half of it?
description: An isosceles triangle is split by a height into two triangles with equal bases and the same height. One of them has area twenty four square units, so the whole triangle has area forty eight square units.
teaching_notes: One idea: the height of an isosceles triangle splits the base in the middle, so the two parts have equal bases, the same height and equal areas. Watch for children who give the whole triangle the area of one part.

video_script.why: The child uses half of base times height to see that two triangles with equal bases and the same height have equal areas, so the whole triangle is double one part.
video_script.substitution: Show that the two parts have equal areas, then add the two equal areas.
video_script.anchor: the isosceles triangle SUB of the book with the line SE at a right angle to UB
video_script.payoff_line: the whole triangle has area forty eight square units
hold_back: the whole triangle has area 48 square units
never_show: the area of the whole triangle, before the step that adds the two parts
maths_rules: triangle SUB is isosceles with SU = SB; SE is perpendicular to UB; area of triangle SEB = 24 square units
in an isosceles triangle the perpendicular from the apex S meets UB at its midpoint, so UE = EB
triangles SUE and SEB have equal bases UE and EB and the same height SE, so equal areas: 1/2 × UE × SE = 1/2 × EB × SE = 24
area of triangle SUB = 24 + 24 = 48 square units
check: folding along SE puts triangle SUE exactly on triangle SEB, so SUB is double SEB: 2 × 24 = 48
video_script.design: One idea: equal bases and the same height give equal areas. The isosceles triangle with its height stays on stage. The fold along the height is the check.
open_questions: The book figure is not in the extracted text. The worklist solution takes SU = SB with S the top corner and E the middle of UB; the picture should be checked against this.
